message.content:
**Hydrogen – Key Physical & Chemical Properties**

| Property | Value / Description |
|----------|---------------------|
| **Atomic number** | 1 |
| **Atomic mass** | 1.008 u (average; ^1H ≈ 1.0079 u, ^2H ≈ 2.014 u, ^3H ≈ 3.016 u) |
| **Electron configuration** | 1s¹ |
| **Electronegativity (Pauling)** | 2.20 |
| **First ionization energy** | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Electron affinity** | –0.754 eV (–72 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| **Boiling point** | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) |
| **Melting point** | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) |
| **Density at STP** | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (≈0.00008988 g cm⁻³) |
| **Molar volume at STP** | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| **State at room temperature** | Gas |
| **Flammability** | Extremely flammable; forms explosive mixtures with air (1–4 % H₂ in air). |
| **Reactivity** | Forms hydrides with metals (e.g., NaH, CaH₂), reacts with halogens (HX), oxidizes to water or oxides. |
| **Isotopes** | ^1H (protium), ^2H (deuterium), ^3H (tritium). Deuterium and tritium are used in nuclear fusion research. |
| **Bonding** | Forms covalent bonds (H₂, H₂O, hydrocarbons), ionic bonds (NaH, CaH₂), and hydrogen bonds (in water, alcohols). |
| **Spectral lines** | Lyman, Balmer, Paschen series in UV/visible/IR; prominent Hα line at 656.3 nm. |
| **Solubility** | Poorly soluble in water (~1.6 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C); more soluble in organic solvents. |
| **Acidity/basicity** | Acts as a weak acid (HF) or base (H₂O → H₃O⁺ + OH⁻). |
| **Oxidation states** | +1 (as in HF, H₂O), –1 (as in LiH, NaH). |
| **Applications** | Fuel (hydrogen fuel cells), industrial feedstock (ammonia synthesis, petroleum refining), laboratory reagent, space propulsion, nuclear fusion research. |

**Summary:**  
Hydrogen is the lightest element, existing as a diatomic gas under normal conditions. It has a high ionization energy, low electron affinity, and is highly flammable. Its isotopes play crucial roles in nuclear fusion and isotope labeling. Hydrogen’s versatile bonding leads to a wide range of compounds, from simple hydrides to complex organic molecules, making it indispensable in chemistry, industry, and energy technologies.
